segments.say: Let's leave mood for a while, and look at attention. A notification buzzes. You glance at it, perhaps you answer, and then you return to what you were doing. It feels like a small, free interruption. Psychologists who study attention have spent years asking what these interruptions actually cost, and their answers are more surprising than you might expect.

One of the best known researchers in this area is Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine. Her approach is unusual. Instead of asking people how they work, she watches them, sometimes with a stopwatch, sometimes by logging their screens, and records exactly how often they switch tasks.

In one experiment, people did writing tasks and were interrupted partway through, while others worked without interruptions. Those who were interrupted finished their tasks just as fast, or faster, but they reported more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort. In other words, people could compensate for the interruption, but it came with a psychological cost.

show.where: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 2008
show.what: The cost of interrupted work: more speed and stress

segments.say: This is a nice example of an effect that doesn't show up in the output, only in the person. The work gets done, so the interruption seems harmless. But the person had to run faster to catch up, and pays for it in tension. Over a day, or a year, such costs may add up, even if no single moment shows them.

Mark has also reported, from observing people in real workplaces, that after a significant interruption it can take on the order of twenty minutes to return to the original task. That figure comes from observations rather than a single controlled experiment, so it's best taken as a rough illustration, not a law. The point is that interruptions don't end when the interruption does.

show.title: Time to return after interruption
show.label: a figure Gloria Mark has described from her field observations of office workers

segments.say: Mark has also tracked how long people stay on one screen before switching. In her studies, the average time on a single screen dropped over the years, from about two and a half minutes in 2004 to roughly forty-seven seconds in more recent measurements. Those figures come from her own samples of office workers, so they don't describe everyone, but the trend is striking.

It's important to be careful with the phrase attention span. Researchers don't have good evidence that human beings are physically losing the ability to concentrate. A more accurate description is that people are switching more often, between tabs, apps and tasks, and that frequent switching is a habit, shaped by the environment, which could be changed.

That last line matters. A popular claim says that people now have an attention span shorter than a goldfish. That claim has no good scientific basis, and it has been traced to a poorly sourced marketing report. It makes for a good headline, but not a true one.

show.title: What we can and can't say
items: People switch screens more often than they used to
Frequent switching is linked to more stress
Interruptions carry costs, even when work gets done
There's no clear proof that attention capacity is shrinking

segments.say: Now to a more surprising claim. Some researchers have suggested that the mere presence of a phone, even switched off and untouched, might reduce your thinking capacity. In 2017, a team led by Adrian Ward at the University of Texas published a study that was widely reported, and is a good case of a finding that needs a second look.

They asked five hundred and twenty students to take attention and reasoning tests, with their phones either on the desk, in a pocket or bag, or in another room. Those with the phone on the desk performed worst on some tests of cognitive capacity, and those with the phone in another room did best. They called it the brain drain effect: the phone, they said, takes up part of your mental resources, even when you aren't using it.

show.where: Journal of the Association for Consumer Research, 2017
show.what: Brain drain: the mere presence of one's own smartphone reduces available cognitive capacity

segments.say: It sounded like a clear and useful finding, and it spread widely. But science moves on. Later teams tried to repeat the study, with larger groups and stricter methods, and several did not find the same pattern. A large replication in 2022 found no reliable effect of the phone's presence on cognitive performance, and the original result is now regarded as uncertain.

show.title: Students in the brain drain study
show.label: tested with their phone on the desk, in a bag, or in another room

segments.say: This is the same story we saw with power posing. An effect that seems intuitive and is easy to explain spreads quickly, and the replication comes quietly, years later. It doesn't mean the idea is definitely false. It means that we shouldn't treat it as established, and should be a little suspicious of results that fit our expectations perfectly.

There is stronger evidence on the notifications themselves. In 2015, Cary Stothart, Ainsley Mitchum and Courtney Yehnert at Florida State University asked people to do a task that required sustained attention. Some received a phone notification, an alert or a call, during the task, which they were told to ignore.

The people who got a notification made more mistakes on the task than those who didn't, even though they hadn't looked at the phone. Simply being alerted was enough to distract them for a while, with performance sagging in a way that was comparable to people who actually used their phones. The size of the effect was modest, but it was consistent.

show.where: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 2015
show.what: The attentional cost of receiving a cell phone notification

segments.say: The study gives a practical reason to turn off alerts that don't matter. Not because phones are evil, but because an alert acts like someone tapping your shoulder, and it can take time to find your place again.

show.title: What notifications seem to do
items: Cost more when the task is difficult

segments.say: A quiet desk, an hourglass, and a phone placed face down at the edge. The research on interruptions suggests that where you put the phone matters less than whether it can reach you, and that a protected stretch of time is one of the most valuable things you can give your work.

To protect your attention, start with a single hour. Silence the notifications, close the extra tabs, and place the phone somewhere that takes effort to reach. If a stray thought arrives, such as an errand or a message to send, write it on a piece of paper and return to the task. That gives the thought a home, so that your mind doesn't have to hold it. Researchers on attention suggest that the first ten minutes are the hardest, and that things get easier after that. One good hour often outweighs several scattered ones.

show.title: Protecting a stretch of deep attention
items: Put the phone in another room
Write down distracting thoughts and return to them later

segments.say: Four terms about attention. Task switching is moving between tasks or screens. Attention residue is the part of your mind that stays on the last task after you switch. Sustained attention is the ability to stay focused over time. And the brain drain claim is the idea that a phone's mere presence uses up thinking capacity, which has not held up.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter

segments.say: You don't have to give up your phone to protect your attention. A single hour of quiet, with alerts silenced, is a good start. Many people find that one deep hour does more than four scattered ones. It's a gift to your future self, and it's one the research gives support for.

show.sub: Guard a small piece of time

segments.say: So what did we learn? That interruptions cost stress even when work is completed. That people switch screens more often, though we can't say that attention spans are shrinking. That the phone-in-the-room effect failed to replicate. And that even ignored notifications can raise errors.
In our next chapter, we'll look at what spreads on social media, and why. A team at MIT studied millions of posts and discovered something uncomfortable about the speed of true and false stories.
